chunks: From him, from Al-Husayn, from Safwan and Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ibn Al-Mughira, from Ibn Bukayr, who said:

Hamaza ibn Humran married the daughter of Bukayr. When he wanted to consummate the marriage with her, they said to him: 'We will not let you enter upon her unless you swear an oath to us.' They did not accept from him an oath of manumission (al-'itq) because he did not consider it significant. Instead, they told him: 'Swear to us by the zihar of the mothers of your children and your female slaves.' So he pronounced zihar from them. He mentioned that to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: 'There is no blame on you; return to them.' If it is said: 'How do they say that zihar by the right hand (yamin) does not take effect?' and it has been narrated in hadiths that expiation (kaffarah) is not obligatory except after the breach (hinth)? Then, if zihar by the right hand were not effective, the expiation would not be obligatory, neither with the breach nor without it.

key_terms.الْحِنْث: The breach (of the zihar oath, triggering expiation)
key_terms.بِيَمِينٍ: By the right hand (referring to the oath of zihar)
key_terms.ظِهَار: Zihar (a form of irrevocable divorce where the husband declares his wife to his back)

ai.seo_question: Is zihar by the right hand considered valid in Shia jurisprudence according to the hadith of Hamaza ibn Humran?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Istibsar* clarifies the jurisprudential status of 'Zihar' when performed via an oath by the 'right hand' (Yamin), a point of contention regarding its binding nature. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) affirmed its validity by ruling that no immediate blame fell upon Hamaza, while the subsequent logical deduction—that expiation (Kaffarah) is contingent upon the breach of the vow—serves as proof that the Zihar was indeed effective (Waqi'). This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on the practical efficacy of oaths in marital contexts, distinguishing it from mere verbal declarations.
